items.title: New York Yankees vs. New York Mets: Gerrit Cole vs. Zac Thornton
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
It’s been an emotional couple of days for the Yankees, with the storybook return of Anthony Volpe on Thursday almost immediately balanced by the weight of yesterday’s 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks. If nothing else, the Yankees won both those games, and stand a good Gerrit Cole start away from likely taking another game, and another series, this afternoon taking on the Mets.

Cole really has one job today — do not give up four home runs. One of the strangest starts you’ll ever see came last weekend in San Diego, where the veteran righty did just that against the Padres, and while they were all solo shots (with a back-to-back-to-back to begin the game), that fateful fourth allowed in the seventh made an ultimately-doomed comeback attempt impossible. Cole’s walk rate is Mars-class, and part of that tradeoff is often pitches in-zone that can be driven with authority, but he’s got to turn those fly balls into outs rather than free handouts to fans. If he does that today, I’m comfortable every time he takes the mound.

Zac Thornton counters for the Mets, a player I’m unfamilar with overall but having quite a solid rookie turn in MLB. A 3.53 ERA is undercut but a FIP almost a full run higher, largely driven by the 2023 fifth-rounder’s low strikeout rate and a high HR rate that xFIP at least believes will be cut down a bit. The Yankee offense is looking a little more professional in recent days, but we’ve also seen how seemingly unknown lefties can torment them in 2026.

Aaron Judge gets a half day off today, as he’ll DH facing the southpaw. This opens right field up for Heliot Ramos and his adventures on defense, while Paul Goldschmidt and Amed Rosario man the corners of the infield. Austin Wells has the catching duties even after playing in last night’s game.

items.title: Brent Headrick is chugging along in uncharted territory
items.author: Kento Mizuno
items.content:
Though the Yankees have endured their fair share of misfortune this year – injuries to several key players come to mind – they’ve also enjoyed some positive surprises. Spencer Jones might be a viable big leaguer! Paul Goldschmidt wasn’t completely toast! Paul Blackburn’s running a sub-2.00 ERA! However, there’s one important development that I feel has flown under the radar at least a little bit, and that is Brent Headrick’s emergence as an elite reliever. 

Those of you following this team closely should need no reminder of how good Headrick has been, but his performance to date stands out even when compared to the rest of the league. Here’s how Brent’s key stats rank among all qualified MLB relievers.

fWAR: (2.2, tied with Trevor Megill)IP: (73.1)ERA: (1.96)ERA-: (47)FIP: (2.31)FIP-: (54, tied with Mason Montgomery)K-BB%: (22.0%)

No matter how you slice it, Headrick’s 2026 performance to date has been nothing short of elite. However, I want to call attention to one stat in particular: his innings count. With about three weeks still remaining in the season, Headrick has already thrown 73.1 innings, the most he’s ever thrown in the majors by far. In fact, even when accounting for his minor league stats, his 2026 workload still stands out.

Headrick did throw 108.1 innings across High-A and Double-A in 2022, followed by 100.2 innings across Triple-A and the majors in 2023. However, that was when he was primarily a swingman, with 35 out of his 58 appearances during that time being starts. Having since moved to a full-time relief role, Headrick accumulated just 69.1 innings ]over 2024 and 2025 across the minors and the majors. In other words, 2026 Headrick has already thrown more innings than his previous two years combined. If I were him, I’d be asking for a hefty raise in the offseason if I wasn’t pre-arb.

With any pitcher — and perhaps doubly so for relievers, who are as a group inherently fickle — a marked increase in workload comes with two red flags: heightened injury risk, and potential decline in performance. I can’t speak on the former, as I’m not a medical professional. However, I can provide some assurance regarding the latter, as despite being worked harder than ever before, Headrick isn’t showing many signs of slowing down.

Yes, it’s true that Headrick’s ERA has risen a bit recently. From the start of the season through July, he posted a 1.30 ERA in 55.1 innings. Since then? A 4.00 mark across 18 innings. However, a look at Headrick’s underlying numbers suggests that this has more to do with bad luck than his workload catching up to him.

If Headrick was truly gassed, we’d expect that to show in several areas of his FanGraphs page. For example, if his stuff was diminished, we’d expect his strikeout rate to decrease and his walk rate to increase. But looking at his splits pre- and post-August, the opposite has happened. Headrick’s actually fanning batters at a higher rate since August 1st (32.2%) than before (29.4%), while his walk rate since (7.4%) is also slightly lower than before (7.8%), even including last night’s two-walk outing. If there has been a decline in Headrick’s stuff, it sure isn’t showing up here.

Of course, it might be that Headrick is allowing harder contact as he runs on fumes. However, the data doesn’t really support this hypothesis either. His hard contact rate was 26.4 percent from March-July, and from the start of August onward that has risen all the way to … 26.5 percent. His batted-ball mix is basically the same, too—he’s generated grounders and fly balls at roughly the same rates. The only difference is that recently more of his fly balls allowed have been leaving the park. His HR/FB rate was a miniscule 3.4 percent prior to August, but since then that’s jumped up to 10.5 percent. However, HR/FB has proven to be a fickle statistic, and very few pitchers have shown the ability to consistently suppress it. Given the fact that a 10.5 percent HR/FB is still below league average, I’m comfortable saying that this shouldn’t be cause for alarm.

The most likely culprit for Headrick’s heightened ERA seems to be worse luck on batted balls. Here’s his 15-game rolling BABIP, through the beginning of play yesterday:

If we superimpose his 15-game rolling ERA- trends on this graph, we can see how closely the two trends coincide:

And if we compare that to his FIP- trends, we can see how Headrick’s core skills have remained consistent despite fluctuations in his surface stats:

So, in my humble opinion, the fact that Headrick’s ERA has risen a bit of late shouldn’t scare you.

At Headrick’s core, he’s still the shutdown reliever he was earlier in the year; he’s just run into a patch of bad luck. Of course, this doesn’t preclude the possibility to Headrick’s workload catching up to him eventually, and we’d be remiss if we didn’t note that his average fastball velocity in September (93.2 mph) is lower than any previous month (below May’s 93.9 mph). It’s not an enormous dip and it’s possible that the adrenaline of the postseason could boost it back up in certain outings.

Nonetheless, Aaron Boone and Matt Blake should of course be monitoring his health closely; going into the playoffs without a fully functioning Headrick would be less than ideal, to say the least. As of now however, Headrick seems to be just fine, and that’s good news for the Yankees as they enter the most crucial part of the season.

items.title: Cam Schlittler’s not the AL MVP … right?
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
Regular readers know that I’ve followed one of the great Cy Young horse races in recent memory, with Cam Schlittler going great start-for-great start with the Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease. We got a little bit of separation this week, as the Athletics touched up Cease for four runs in five innings on Monday, and then Schlittler allowed just a solo shot in seven frames against the Rockies on Tuesday. Cam has crept just ahead by fWAR, enjoys a considerable lead in bWAR, and right now I think would end up at the top of most voters’ ballots.

But something struck me in the aftermath of Cam’s night against Colorado, the same night that Aaron Judge returned to the lineup. Cam Schlittler isn’t just the Cy Young favorite, but he’s built himself an MVP case. No pitcher has won the award since Clayton Kershaw for the 2014 Dodgers, and the last AL winner was 2011 Justin Verlander. Yordan Alvarez is in the hunt for the first Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera, Bobby Witt Jr. is probably the best overall player in the league, and if Junior Caminero tops the AL in home runs and plays on the Junior Circuit’s best team, he probably gets his share of votes too.

And yet here’s the thing: Cam stacks up fairly against all three of them!

Let’s take Yordan, who I think has the inside track on the award right now. Schlittler’s 0.1 fWAR back, a difference that is literally negligible, and more than three-quarters of a win better by bWAR. Alvarez’s candidacy is based around the Triple Crown, probably being the best hitter in baseball, and dragging what we thought was a finally-deflated Houston Astros team to a division title. Crappy AL West or not, that is exactly the blueprint for an MVP, if one for a slightly older voter.

Should Alvarez not win the Triple Crown, he loses a bit of his case, though he’s likely still the best hitter in the game on a division winner, one who will have played in the neighborhood of 155 games. That’s the big thing both undercutting Witt’s MVP claim while bolstering his position as best all-around player — the Kansas City shortstop has only played 128 games at time of writing, yet leads the league in fWAR and bWAR among position players. With a solid-but-not-spectacular 18 homers and 124 wRC+, the parts of his game beyond hitting are doing the heavy lifting there as well. All that and the fact that the Royals are so bad work against him when it comes to end of season awards though, and Bobby seems cursed to be the Dave Stieb of shortstops.

Junior Caminero, fittingly, is the junior candidate in this slate, trailing the rest of the field pretty clearly by WAR. The home run totals (an AL-leading 39 as of the time of writing) and the Rays’ season of devil magic help fill in some of the gaps that would otherwise leave him a downballot vote-getter that helped a lot of people’s fantasy teams, and in the end he might be just that. Great season, frightening player, but more of a top-five finisher than taking home the hardware.

Cam Schlittler leads the entire AL in bWAR, position players or no. He is virtually tied for third in fWAR. Perhaps most key to his case is the way this Yankee team has been beaten up, with four of his fellow starters seeing IL time this year. The Yankees came into the season with more starting pitching than they needed, and it ended up being just enough, with a chunk of that being because Schlittler has been so reliable, not missing a single start. Virtually every member of the regular starting lineup, save Ben Rice and Paul Goldschmidt, has been injured or demoted in some form this year, and the Opening Day center fielder, DH, and second baseman might not even finish the season on the big-league roster.

Through all that, the consistent, balancing force has been Cam’s right arm every five days.

MVPs are built on a combination of statistical success and compelling narrative — Aaron Judge’s 2022 was at that point his career-best season, but the chase for 62 is what pushed him over the line. Cam has the total value arguments, and certainly if you can make a compelling case for MVP you have to be the favorite for the Cy Young. Moreover, him being at 25 the stabilizing energy for a team that could very well have completely fallen apart, he may end up higher than you think on the ballot that means the most.

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Charlie Keller
items.author: Jonathan Farrar
items.content:
Before he was a star for the Yankees, Charlie Keller was a small-town boy on a Maryland farm. In a truly poetic life journey, that is exactly the life that he would return to after playing 13 years in the major leagues, with a gap year in there to serve as a merchant marine.

September 12, 1916 (Middletown, MD) May 23, 1990 (Frederick, MD) 1939-1943, 1945-1949, 1952

Keller came of age working on the family farm and eventually became a standout athlete at Middletown High School, just a bit outside Frederick, Maryland. While at Middletown, Keller was a state champion in track while playing baseball, basketball, and soccer. With the book smarts to match his athletic ability, Keller went to the University of Maryland on scholarship. While in undergrad, Keller played both basketball and baseball at the varsity level, gradually turning into one of the greatest Terps to ever grace the diamond.

Baseball became the sport that the right-hand-throwing and lefty-swinging Keller would come to dominate. After an impressive showing both in school and during a semi-professional league, Yankees scout Gene McCann signed Keller to a contract just before the start of the 1937 season.

At 20 years old, Keller’s professional journey officially began as a member of the Newark Bears. Upon reporting to spring training, the Yankees informed Keller they planned to play him in right field, a new position. The Yankees also spent the 1937 season trying to get the stout lefty to focus on pulling the baseball. In his first taste of pro ball, Keller slashed .353/.431/.541 with 13 home runs, 14 triples, and 34 doubles. Keller ditched the pull approach ahead of the 1938 season and went on to win the batting title with a .353 average while also leading the league in runs and hits. For his efforts, he was named both the International League Rookie of the Year and Minor League Player of the Year of 1938.

Skipper Joe McCarthy and the Yankees gave Keller his first taste of pro ball in 1939. After missing the start of the season due to injury, the rookie, who was now primarily playing left field, finally made his debut at the end of April. The rookie struggled to find playing time over the first few months of the summer, but starting in August, the kid caught fire and would force his way into the lineup through the end of the regular season and into the Fall Classic.

New York swept the Cincinnati Reds in the 1939 World Series as Keller had a team-high .438 average, to go along with three home runs and six RBIs. The rookie’s triple in the ninth inning of Game 1 (as seen below) led to a walk-off hit by Bill Dickey and set the tone for the series. In the Game 4 clincher, he came around to score in the 10th inning on a chaotic play started by a Joe DiMaggio hit. An E9 enabled Keller to come home, and as he did so, he collided with Reds catcher Ernie Lombardi. The dazed Lombardi was slow to come to his senses and by the time he’d done so, DiMaggio had scored himself. The sweep was completed shortly afterward.

The 1940 season was the start of a legendary run for Keller. He was an All-Star in 1940, leading the league in base on balls while batting .286 with 21 home runs. The Yankees would miss the playoffs that season after finishing 88-66 and third in the American League.

Keller had one of, if not his best, seasons in 1941. He hit .298 and posted career highs in home runs with 33 big flies and 122 RBIs. Keller finished fifth in the MVP vote and was an All-Star for the second time. The Yankees found themselves back in the World Series and Keller impressed again, batting .389 while driving in five runs and scoring another five himself. In the most memorable highlight from that series, Yankees batter Tommy Henrich Brooklyn catcher Mickey Owen both missed a wicked pitch from Hugh Casey, and what would have been a strikeout for the end of a series-tying Dodgers win in Game 4 instead continued with Henrich on first. DiMaggio singled and Keller became the one to really twist the screws with a two-run double that put the Yankees ahead, 5-4.

Both the Yankees and Keller had a bit of a disappointing year, for their standards, in 1942. Keller posted a .292/.417/.513 slash line behind 26 home runs and a career-high 14 stolen bases. The Yankees made the World Series but lost to the Cardinals 4-1; Keller was held to four hits in five games, though two were homers.

The 1943 campaign saw Keller get his third All-Star selection as he led the league in base on balls again and OPS with a .922 and OPS+ of 168. The Yankees again found themselves facing the red bird of St. Louis in the World Series. This time, the Yankees prevailed in five games, giving Keller his third ring in five seasons.

Then, in January of 1944, everything changed for Keller as he was commissioned into the U.S. Maritime Service. Keller would serve in the Pacific for the next 20 months. In August of 1945, Keller returned to the Yankees for the final stretch of the season. Despite still having his sea legs under him, Keller hit .301 with 10 home runs in 44 games as the Yankees finished third in the league.

The 1946 Yankees also finished in third place and missed the playoffs, but Keller returned to his pre-war form and was again an All-Star. On the season, Keller launched 30 home runs, driving in 101, and drawing 113 base on balls to give him his fifth career season to exceed 100+ walks.

Keller was still in top form for the first third of the 1947 season. Entering June, he was leading the league in several offensive categories and would earn his fifth All-Star selection in just a few weeks. Little did anyone know, but a small tweak of his back while taking a swing forever changed his career. Keller ended up having surgery to remove a slipped disk in July. Keller missed the rest of the season and had to watch from the dugout as his teammates took down the Dodgers in seven games to win the 1947 World Series.

The legendary swing from King Kong Keller was never the same. Despite trying to work his way back into form, Keller struggled in 1948 and 1949. Over those two campaigns, he slashed .262/.378/.405 with only 9 home runs in 143 games. The man once a lock for 600 at-bats and 100 walks was no more. In another bittersweet moment, Keller watched his teammates win the 1949 World Series.

As a Yankee, Keller finished his career with a slash line of .286/.410/.518 with an OPS of .928 and a WAR of 42.3 in 1066 games. His .410 career OBP ranks him top 5 all-time in Yankees franchise history. Keller also averaged roughly three walks for every two strikeouts, which is crazy for a slugger like him.

The Tigers signed Keller after the Yankees released him in 1949. Keller spent the 1950 and 1951 seasons mostly appearing as a pinch-hitter for the Tigers. In limited action over those two years, Keller hit .283 with five home runs. The Yankees brought Keller home for the 1952 season. However, after only one at-bat in 1952, the Yankees released Keller and his playing career was over.

After his playing days ended, Keller returned to Maryland and started Yankeeland Farm. He remained on the farm for the remainder of his days except for when the Yankees asked him to don the pinstripes again as a coach during the 1957 season. Keller stuck with the team under Casey Stengel through the end of the 1959 season. While he served as the team’s first base coach, the team lost the 1957 World Series but get revenge and win the 1958 World Series in a rematch with the Milwaukee Braves. That ring gave Keller his sixth as a Yankee.

Though it was cut short, Keller’s peak was one remarkable run. Three modern players who can help put his career into perspective, according to Baseball Reference’s Similar Batters, are Juan Soto, Josh Hamilton, and Cody Bellinger. Another comparison is Bryce Harper as the athletic, converted catcher, super-slugging lefty. In an organization with some of the greatest of all time, Keller might truly be the greatest what-if in pinstripe history.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: Yankees Rivalry Roundup: Rays walk off Astros in series opener
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
The Yankees kicked off the Subway Series with a win, scoring six on the Mets and managing to hold on despite the anomaly that was Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick both struggling on the same night. David Bednar came in for the five-out save and got the job done, escaping a bases-loaded jam in the eighth before getting a game-ending double-play out of Juan Soto in the ninth. While they were handling business in the Bronx, they were also scoreboard watching with several key games going on simultaneously — so let’s see what the result of those out of town scores were.

Tampa Bay Rays (88-59) 3, Houston Astros (75-73) 1

The Rays looked like they could’ve slipped up and lost this game ceding some ground to New York, but they came around to walk it off instead. Houston had their chances against Drew Rasmussen, scattering eight hits against the Rays’ ace, but the only run they managed to score came in the fourth inning when Isaac Paredes doubled with one out and Daulton Varsho singled to put runners on the corners. Yainer Diaz hit a ball hard to second base, and while Ritchie Palacios made a fantastic play on the ball flipping it to the shortstop quickly enough for the force out keeping the potential double play alive, Diaz managed to beat the throw letting the run count. However, several other innings were cut short by double plays that did get converted, and the Rays tied the game back up in the fifth when Victor Mesa Jr. launched a home run to lead off the inning.

Things stayed quiet until the bottom of the ninth, when the Rays got the winning run aboard on an Aranda double before Junior Caminero stepped up to the plate. Bryan Abreu chose to start him off with a fastball up in the zone and Caminero made him pay, ripping a walk-off two-run shot to left.

The win not only kept the Rays three games ahead of the Yankees in the standings, but it clinched a playoff spot for Tampa Bay — the first team to secure a spot in the 2026 Postseason. The Brewers would join them a little later in the night with a blowout win on their part, but the Rays are, for now, the only American League team holding a ticket to the dance.

Boston Red Sox (80-68) 2, Kansas City Royals (66-82) 3: The Yankees did gain some ground on Friday, as the Red Sox fell behind early to Kansas City and couldn’t dig themselves out of the hole. Carter Jensen led off the game against Sonny Gray with a double and later scored on a Salvador Perez single to left, and then the Royals added to their lead in the third as Isaac Collins and Jensen hit back-to-back doubles followed by a Vinnie Pasquantino RBI single. Mickey Gasper got Boston on the scoreboard in the fifth with a solo shot, and after Adley Rutschman walked Wilyer Abreu doubled him in to cut the lead to 3-2. The Sox struck out from there though, and Boston would get just one hit the rest of the way stranding a Trevor Story double in the eighth.

Chicago White Sox (75-72) 3, St. Louis Cardinals (73-75) 7: The White Sox are squandering their advantage in the Central, losing their fourth straight game. The Cardinals scored a run in each of the first three innings, but they delivered the knockout punch in the fifth as Jordan Walker, Alec Burleson, Joshua Báez, and Leo Bernal chained consecutive hits to drive in three runs. The Cardinal bullpen dealt with some traffic on the basepaths but managed to limit Chicago to just one run in the final 4.2 innings. Chase Meidroth showed up for the Southsiders, launching two home runs to briefly keep them within arm’s reach of St. Louis.

Cleveland Guardians (75-73) 5, Minnesota Twins (69-78) 2: Chicago’s faltering opens the door for Cleveland, who moved to within a half-game of first place after taking this one against the Twins. The game was tied at two in the ninth when a wild pitch and a two-run double from Brayan Rocchio put them up three in a heartbeat. Cade Smith entered looking for the save and got the job done quickly with a double-play ball to erase a one-out single from Trevor Larnach.

Toronto Blue Jays (73-75) 4, Baltimore Orioles (72-76) 7: The O’s jumped out to a 6-0 lead in this game, scoring five in the second inning with two-run hits from Colton Cowser and Dylan Beavers leading the procession. Toronto had a rally in them in the ninth, scoring two runs on a Brett Bateman homer before George Springer and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. hit singles to bring the tying run to the plate. Unfortunately for Toronto this all came with two outs, and when Baltimore went back to their ‘pen summoning Rico Garcia to pitch he managed to get Alejandro Kirk to ground out to end it.

Texas Rangers (72-76) 1, Arizona Diamondbacks (79-69) 9: Two innings were all Arizona needed to put up a nine-spot on Texas in a rematch of the 2023 World Series. A trio of doubles in the fifth led to four runs scoring for the Diamondbacks, followed by Corbin Carroll and Nolan Arenado launching back-to-back homers in the sixth to drive the dagger home. Justin Martinez had the highlight of the night for the pitching staff, tossing an immaculate inning in the top of the sixth shutting the door on any potential response from Texas after Arizona took the lead.

items.title: Can Anthony Volpe’s changes help him take advantage of Yankees’ opportunity?
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
To say that Anthony Volpe’s MLB career to this point has been a disappointment would be an understatement. He has certainly had his moments, but a first-round pick producing an 85 wRC+ in parts of four campaigns is definitely not what you want, 2023 Gold Glove notwithstanding. Having said that, it’s impossible to deny that the kid is a hard worker and seems determined to make it work at the highest level.

After the Yankees promoted George Lombard Jr. immediately following the Trade Deadline, Volpe was sent to the minor leagues. He didn’t use the time to play around or publicly complain about fate and harsh roster decisions. No, he used it to train, work, and try to become the best version of himself he could be.

Volpe made adjustments at the plate, increased his focus, and started to perform and put up numbers in Scranton. From August 7th to September 7th—exactly a month’s worth of stats—he hit .284/.381/.642 with a 1.023 OPS, a 159 wRC+, 10 home runs, seven doubles, and eight steals as well. Additionally, he worked in other infield positions other than shortstop, increasing his versatility by spending the bulk of his time at the keystone, plus a few games at the hot corner.

Of course, Volpe has raked in the minor leagues before; that’s part of what excited Yankees fans about him in the first place, especially in 2022. The challenge will be doing it in the majors, but he got off to a solid start with a 3-for-4 performance on Thursday against the Rockies as a second baseman filling in for the injured Jazz Chisholm Jr. One of those hits was a grand slam to the Short Porch, and on the night, he drove in five while stealing a base.

Nobody rational is losing their minds over one game, but there are some changes he implemented in his batting stance and timing mechanism that are worth discussing. A Twitter user named Victor posted a video comparing Volpe’s stance earlier in 2026 and one from Thursday’s game, and the difference is quite clear.

The swing seems much more explosive. Obviously, being healthy after offseason labrum surgery helps, but the infielder seems to have incorporated a step-back move to fully load and then unleash his power on pitches. The swing path also looks different, in this lone example, at least. Well, for a day, at least, it all worked, but his Triple-A performance this past month can’t be completely ignored, either.

Since they have a pressing need at second with Chisholm out and he only made three appearances at the hot corner in the minors, Volpe is expected to be used almost exclusively at the keystone in the short-term, although it’s nice to know he could be an emergency option across the infield if something comes up. All things considered, the former Gold Glover does have some exciting potential to help the Yankees in the next week or two. He just has to take advantage of his opportunity.

Although it almost feels as though Volpe has been around forever, the man is still just 25 years old. Fate and his own hard work have given him a chance to put himself on the map again—especially as the Yankees enter an offseason where Chisholm may depart in free agency. It’s likely to be a brief window in terms of immediate 2026 impact, so he needs to show something.

Whatever happens with Volpe when Chisholm returns is anyone’s guess, because the latter is expected to slide back to his starting role once he’s deemed healthy enough to play. For the former, however, it all starts with making a good impression in the handful of MLB games he will be given in the next couple weeks, and we aren’t talking exclusively about stats: how his swing looks, how he fares in adversity, how he looks with the glove, and his level of intensity and focus will all be evaluated. It’s one thing to have a big game with the cellar-dwelling Rockies in town; it’s quite another to do so against tougher foes, especially if he remains a factor for the Rays series from September 22-24 (though Chisholm could be back by then).

Volpe has a brief but meaningful chance in front of him, regardless of whether or not it results in a spot on the postseason roster, or if there’s a potential impact on 2027 plans. Those are discussions for another time. The here and now is all that matters for Volpe.

items.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 9/12/26
items.author: Andrew Mearns
items.content:
Yesterday was the 25th anniversary of 9/11. Today is my parents’ 45th anniversary. Tomorrow is my cousin’s birthday. Time marches on, huh? I know yesterday was hard for many people in this fandom (and beyond), so hopefully we can help today, tomorrow, and beyond feel a little more normal.

Today on the site, Andrés will look at what Anthony Volpe has done in the past month to prepare himself for the opportunity to fill in for the injured Jazz Chisholm Jr. at second, Madison will run through the Rivalry Roundup, and Jonathan will celebrate the 110th birthday of underrated Yankees masher Charlie Keller. Later, Josh will discuss Cam Schlittler and the AL MVP conversation, Kento will give Brent Headrick his flowers, and Matt will remember the game in 1990 in which the Yankees were improbably allowed to score 10 unearned runs.

New York Yankees vs. New York Mets

TV: YES Network, SNY, MLB Network

Venue: Yankee Stadium, Bronx, NY

1. Who will end up leading the American League in homers: Yordan Alvarez (38), Junior Caminero (40), or Ben Rice (37)?

2. Any college football matchups on the top of your docket for today?

items.title: Yankees news: Remembering September 11th
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
ABC7 | Sam Ryan: Yesterday was the 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks, and baseball played somewhat of a role in helping New York and the nation emotionally recover. Several players from 2001 were part of the pregame remembrances ahead of the Subway Series game on Friday. Players from both teams also took time to tell what they remember from those times 25 years ago.

MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: Among those pregame moments, the Yankees had Brielle Saracini and Sean McGuire, who were both children when they lost parents on 9/11 (and later married), throw out the first pitches. However, it was not Saracini’s first time up close with the Yankees, as Derek Jeter and the team invited her to a game back in 2001 after she had written a letter to the team as a 10-year old shortly after the tragedy. Ahead of Friday’s game, they reunited and both remembered their experiences.

New York Post | Dan Martin: The Yankees made a couple lower-profile additions to try and shore up their bullpen in recent weeks, and one of them was former AL Rookie of the Year Michael Fulmer. In this Subway Series, he’s facing the team that drafted him years ago, eventually trading him to the Tigers for Yoenis Cespedes in 2015. However, he’s now on the other side of the city and has gotten off to a decent start in the Bronx.

items.title: Yankees take opener over Mets after strong outing from Carlos Rodón
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
A Subway Series game on the 25th anniversary of September 11th was always going to bring about some pomp and circumstance and a chance for New Yorkers of all fandoms to come together and pay tribute.

However once the first pitch is thrown, both sets of fans want their team to win above all else. In the series opener, the Yankees’ fans were the ones that got to celebrate.

On the mound, Carlos Rodón was very good. He ended up going 6.1 innings, allowing two runs (only one earned) on three hits and a walk, while striking out eight. At the plate, the Yankees got to Mets’ starter Nolan McLean for a couple runs, including a big three-run homer from Cody Bellinger. That proved enough to give the Yankees a 6-4 win in the Subway Series opener against the mets.

The Yankees started out the game in close to perfect fashion. Ben Rice and Bellinger started with singles, followed by an Aaron Judge walk to load the bases. The inning didn’t turn out as good as it could’ve after that, though. Spencer Jones brought home one run with a single, but the bases were stranded loaded, including an inning-ending double play by George Lombard Jr.

Naturally right after that, the Mets immediately answered. Mark Vientos walked and two batters later, Marcus Semien singled, with a Jones misplay allowing them to move up a base each. That error would allow Vientos to score on a ground out, tying the game.

However, the Yankees’ offense had a reply waiting. While the first two hitters of the second went down in order, Anthony Volpe continued his nice start since returning with a single. Ben Rice followed that with a single, having used ABS to successfully overturned a strike three. That kept the inning going for Bellinger, who took a three-run shot out to right field.

Rodón settled in a bit after that and the Yankees eventually tacked on more. Rice led off the bottom of the fifth with a homer. They again missed out on an opportunity to add more, though.

In the sixth inning, Rodón got one out before allowing a single, which would be the end of his day. Paul Blackburn came in and got two outs, but a walk and a single got the Mets a run back. Brent Headrick came in for him and got out of the inning with a nifty catch on a comebacker.

Headrick then came back out for the eighth, but much like Blackburn in the inning before, he got himself into some trouble. A single and two walks loaded the bases with just one out, leading to Aaron Boone going to David Bednar for a potential five-out save. He got the first two, but a Semien sacrifice fly scored one run before the inning ended.

With the Yankees’ lead dwindling, they were in need of some insurance in the ninth. Luis García Jr. and Jones each hit a single, with George Lombard Jr. then bunting them up a base. Ryan McMahon then dropped in a single that only scored one run, as pinch runner José Caballero had to hold up to make sure the ball wasn’t caught. The hit did provide some insurance, but it did end up keeping the Yankees from more in the inning.

With Bednar back on for the ninth, the inning got off to an iffy start when A.J. Ewing hit a laser of a home run into the second deck in right field. A Francisco Lindor single later in the inning meant that Juan Soto came to the plate as the potential tying run, as the narrative decided not to use subtext. However, Bednar got Soto to ground into a game-ending double play to take round one of the set.

The Subway Series will continue tomorrow at 1:35 pm ET. Gerrit Cole and Zac Thornton are expected to be the starting pitchers.
